newsitem.title: UK: Stg soft in Europe, little support from UK data.
newsitem.headline: Stg soft in Europe, little support from UK data.

text.p: Sterling slipped against the mark and dollar in morning Europe, softened by a retreat in dollar/mark and a negative reaction to mixed UK retail sales and GDP data.

UK sales rose 0.1 percent in April, below expectations of a 0.3 rise. But the annual rise was 4.7 percent, above a forecast of 4.1. The figure for March was also revised up sharply to 0.7 percent from the preliminary 0.3 announced previously.

"While it looks weaker over the month, there have obviously been a lot of backward revisions and 4.7 percent year-on-year is likely to be viewed as uncomfortably strong by the Bank of England," said Alex Garrard, economist at UBS in London.
UK first quarter GDP showed a similar picture with the quarterly rise of 0.9 percent slightly below forecasts and the annual rate as expected at 3.0 percent.
While analysts saw the data as further fuel for UK rate hike speculation and supportive for sterling, currency dealers greeted the data by taking the pound even lower after earlier falls.

"I don't think the data was too instrumental, it was a bit mixed," said a UK bank dealer. "This is more disappointment on the technical side after it failed to push through some key levels yesterday."
Sterling/mark lost nearly three pfennigs in morning trade, retreating from levels just shy of 2.80 marks pre-data to just above 2.77 marks closer to the midsession.
By 1019 GMT it stood at 2.7740/50 marks against 2.7910/20 late Wednesday in Europe.

Dealers said the weaker pound was due mainly to a retreat in dollar/mark amid a stronger than expected German Ifo business survey for April, offsetting earlier news of lower than expected growth in Germany's M3 money supply data for April.
"People are starting to see 2.80 marks and $1.65-66 as high enough. Higher rates are expected which is supporting but there isn't much mileage anymore on the upside," said the UK bank dealer.
Analysts are expecting a UK rate hike in the near future but not until later in June, when the new Labour government is expected to announce its first budget.

"The Bank of England will probably increase rates further but the logistics means it will come after the budget rather than before," Andrew Snowball, economist at the Co-operative Bank in London, told Reuters Financial Television.
Against the dollar, the pound was trading at $1.6382/92 against $1.6472/82 late Wednesday after touching a four-month high just short of $1.66 early yesterday.
